text: A Phosphoramide-Based Electrolyte with High Affinity towards Li+ and Low Polysulfide Solubility Enables High-Performance Lithium–Sulfur Batteries Jie Ren a,1, Congkai Sun a,1, Wenbin Gong b, Ji Zhou c, Shang Chen c, Manyun Wang c, Christopher W.

Bielawski d,e, Jianxin Geng a,* a State Key Laboratory of Advanced Separation Membrane Materials, Tianjin Key Laboratory of Advanced Fibers and Energy Storage, School of Material Science and Engineering, Tiangong University, No. 399 BinShuiXi Road, XiQing District, Tianjin 300387, China b School of Physics and Energy, Xuzhou University of Technology, No.2 Lishui Road, Yunlong District, Xuzhou 221018, China c State Key Laboratory of Organic-Inorganic Composites, Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Soft Matter Science and Engineering, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, No. 15 North Third Road East, Chaoyang District, Beijing 100029, China d Center for Multidimensional Carbon Materials (CMCM), Institute for Basic Science (IBS), Ulsan 44919, Republic of Korea e Department of Chemistry, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), Ulsan 44919, Republic of Korea A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Li−S batteries Li+ solvation structure Shuttle effect Solid-electrolyte interphase A B S T R A C T The polysulfide shuttle effect and the growth of Li dendrites are detrimental to the practical use of lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries.
Here, we show that these challenges can be eliminated with hexamethylphosphoramide (HMPA) as a co-solvent.
HMPA shows strong coordination interaction with Li+ and thus preferentially remains in the inner sheath of the Li+ solvation structure.

The solvation structure not only minimizes the solubility of poly­ sulfides but also generates a LiF-rich solid-electrolyte interphase, which are responsible to the suppression of polysulfide shuttle effect and the elimination of Li dendrites, respectively.
As a result, HMPA-based electrolytes enable Li//Li symmetric cells to exhibit long cycling lifetimes of up to 600 h at 5 mA cm−2 along with signifi­ cantly reduced polarization.
Moreover, Li–S cells containing the HMPA-based electrolyte also display marked enhancement in cycling stability (e.g., 619.6 mAh g−1 after 300 cycles at 0.2 C).
These results are superior to those measured for control cells that contain a conventional electrolyte.
The concepts and method described herein may be extended to benefit other types of energy storage devices that use active metals as anodes. 1.
Introduction Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries are regarded as highly promising, next-generation energy storage devices due to the intrinsic advantages bestowed by sulfur and lithium.
Sulfur possesses a high theoretical specific capacity (1675 mAh g−1) while being abundant, inexpensive, and friendly to the environment [1].
Lithium also features a high theoretical specific capacity (3860 mAh g−1) along with a low density (0.534 g cm−3) and a low electrochemical potential (−3.04 V versus standard hydrogen electrode).
As such, the theoretical energy density of Li–S batteries is high, with reported estimates of 2600 Wh kg−1 [2].
Despite these advantages, the practical use of Li–S batteries is hin­ dered by the notorious polysulfide shuttle effect and the unwanted growth of Li dendrites.
These issues not only degrade device performance but can compromise safety.

The shuttle effect can be mitigated by a number of strategies, including I) confinement of poly­ sulfides within the cathode host materials via physical and/or chemical adsorption [3–5], II) covalent attachment of sulfur to the cathode hosts [6–9], III) controlling the sulfur as smaller allotropes [10], and IV) adding a layer to the separator or inserting an interlayer into the device to prevent diffusion of the polysulfides to the anode [11–13].

A number of strategies have also been explored as solutions to the issues associated with the Li metal anode, such as the I) construction of artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers to protect the Li metal anode [14–18] and II) employment of three-dimensional host materials to regulate the deposition of metallic Li [19–22].

A commonly used electrolyte in Li–S batteries is a solution of lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI, usually 1 M) with a LiNO3 additive (usually ≤0.5 M) in a mixture of 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) (1:1 v/ v).

Unfortunately, Li–S batteries that contain this electrolyte experience premature corrosion of the Li metal anode and severely suffer from the shuttle effect in part because the ethereal solvents facilitate the disso­ lution of polysulfides [25–28].
As such, new electrolyte systems have been proposed, including those that feature high concentrations of Li+ or are based on ionic liquids [29,30].
In the former, the high salt con­ centration minimizes the fraction of free solvent molecules and thus attenuates its capability to dissolve polysulfides.
Polysulfides are poorly soluble in certain ionic liquids due to a mismatch in polarity.
However, these electrolytes often afford devices with sluggish cathode kinetics, which ultimately compromises rate capability.

Highly solvating elec­ trolytes (HSEs), which utilize high donor-number (DN) solvents, are a promising alternative as they have been shown to accelerate cathode reaction kinetics, enhance sulfur utilization, and alleviate deleterious surface passivation effects [31–33].
However, high DN solvents can facilitate the dissolution of polysulfides and thus aggravate the poly­ sulfide shuttle effect.
The standing challenge has been to enhance the Li+ solvation capability of the electrolyte while suppressing polysulfide dissolution.
Here, we report that hexamethylphosphoramide (HMPA) is a viable solution to this longstanding challenge.
HMPA has a high DN value (37.8 kcal mol−1) and forms robust Li+ solvation structures.
Moreover, it was discovered that integrating HMPA with a common, ether-based electrolyte minimizes the solubility of polysulfides and thus effectively suppresses the shuttle effect.
HMPA also enables Li+ to form contact ion pairs (CIPs) and ion aggregates (AGGs) that lead to homogeneous LiFrich SEI layers on the surfaces of Li metal anodes.

These beneficial ef­ fects manifested in high performance devices as Li//Li symmetric cells containing a HMPA-based electrolyte generated a significantly lower polarization voltage in stripping/plating cycling tests (for more than 600 h at 5 mA cm−2) when compared to analogous cells that contained a conventional electrolyte (c.f., 0.06 vs. 0.25 V, respectively).

Further­ more, Li–S cells containing a HMPA-based electrolyte also exhibited improved performance metrics when compared to cells that contained a conventional electrolyte, including a markedly improved rate capability (e.g., 606.4 vs. 181.5 mAh g−1 at 2 C) and a greatly increased cycling stability (e.g., 619.6 vs. 295.2 mAh g−1 after 300 cycles at 0.2 C).

Our work establishes a new method for overcoming the longstanding issues that have limited the practicality of Li–S batteries and, because the method is straightforward and cost-effective, it is poised for adaption to other energy storage devices. 2.
Results and Discussion 2.1.
Electrolyte design The DN number of HMPA was measured to be 37.8 kcal mol−1 via nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy (see Fig.

S1 for de­ tails), which is significantly higher than the values of commonly used ether-based solvents (e.g., 20.0 and 18.0 kcal mol−1 for DME and DOL [34], respectively) and amide-based solvents (e.g., 26.6, 27.3, 28.0, and 29.0 kcal mol−1 for N,N-dimethylformamide, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, N,N-dimethylacetamide, and 1,3-dimethyl-2-imidazolidinone [35–37], respectively).
The solubility of the electrolyte salt, LiTFSI, in HMPA was measured to be approximately one tenth of the value in DME (ca. 0.6 M and 5.8 M, respectively).
As such, the solubility of polysulfides in a HMPA-based electrolyte should be reduced due to the common ion effect [38,39].
These unique features were envisioned to promote sulfur cathode reaction kinetics and suppress the polysulfide shuttle effect.
The effects of HMPA on other aspects of sulfur cathode chemistry has been recently reported [40].
A molecular electrostatic potential analysis indicated that the negatively charged regions of HMPA and DME are located on their respective oxygen atoms (Fig. 1a).
Compared with DME, the oxygen atom of HMPA exhibits a higher electrostatic potential, which, in turn, should manifest in a relatively high affinity toward metal cations, such as Li+.

When used as a co-solvent with DOL to dissolve LiTFSI, which is poorly soluble in HMPA, the formation of contact ion pairs (CIPs) and ion aggregates (AGGs) between Li cations and TFSI anions becomes plausible (Fig. 1b, left).
Meanwhile, the relatively high affinity of HMPA for Li+ should cause HMPA to localize in the inner sheath of a Li+ sol­ vation structure, leading to a reduced number of free HMPA molecules.

These effects should not only suppress its capability to dissolve poly­ sulfides but also facilitate the formation of a LiF-rich SEI layer on the surface of the anode along with homogeneous Li deposition.
With these considerations in mind, an electrolyte that consisted of LiTFSI, DOL, and DME was selected as a comparative control (Fig. 1b, right).
In the control, Li+ should be separated from TFSI−because LiTFSI exhibits a relatively high solubility in DME.
Such solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIPs) typically result in the formation of SEI layers with a rela­ tively poor content of LiF as well as uneven Li deposition [41].
More­ over, the relatively low affinity of ethers (vs.
HMPA) for Li+ should minimize solvent localization and thus promote polysulfide dissolution.
Indeed, Li–S batteries that are prepared with DOL/DME electrolytes often exhibit a pronounced polysulfide shuttle effect as well as signifi­ cant Li dendrite formation. 2.2.
Li+ solvation structure elucidation The coordination structures formed between a Li cation and a molecule of HMPA, DME, or DOL is shown in Fig. 2a.
The oxygen atom of each solvent molecule features a negative electrostatic potential and therefore preferentially coordinates to Li+.
The binding energy released by complexation of Li+ with HMPA (2.86 eV) was calculated to be higher than the values calculated for DME (2.75 eV) and DOL (1.68 eV) (Fig. 2b).

To determine the optimal loading of HMPA, a series of electrolytes were prepared by dissolving LiTFSI (1 M) in mixtures of DOL and HMPA that contained a LiNO3 additive (2 wt%) and different HMPA loadings (4, 6, 8, or 10 vol% of the total volume).
The corresponding electrolytes were denoted as DOL/HMPA-4, DOL/HMPA-6, DOL/HMPA-8, and DOL/HMPA-10, respectively.
The control electrolyte was prepared by dissolving LiTFSI (1 M) in a 1:1 v/v mixture of DOL and DME containing LiNO3 (2 wt%) and denoted as DOL/DME.
Ion conductivity (σ) and Li+ transference number (tLi +) values were initially measured to evaluate ion transport characteristics (see Fig.
S2 for the raw data).
While the σ is affected by the constituent cations (e.g., Li+) and anions (e.g., TFSI−), the tLi + represents the contribution of only the Li+ to the σ value.
Both the σ and tLi + values were found to be correlated with the HMPA loading, with maximum values of 4.51 mS cm−1 and 0.88, respectively, achieved at a HMPA loading of 6 vol% (Fig. 2c and d).

The enhancement in Li+ transport was consistent with the reduced activation energy calculated for the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte when compared to that calculated for the DOL/DME electrolyte (14.1 vs. 19.3 kJ mol−1) (Fig.

Moreover, the optimal Li+ transport properties of the electrolyte containing HMPA are superior to those measured for electrolytes that use amide additives as the corresponding tLi + values typically range between 0.43 and 0.66 [42–44].
The superior Li+ transport properties can be attributed to the solvation structure of Li+ formed with HMPA.
Further increasing the loading of HMPA led to reduced σ and tLi + values as the excess HMPA increased the viscosity of the electrolyte.
Therefore, an HMPA loading of 6 vol% was determined to be optimal and the DOL/HMPA-6 was used as the electrolyte in the following experiments.
The Li+ solvation structures formed in the electrolytes were first evaluated using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
The radial relative density calculated for the oxygen atoms around the constituent Li+ ions is shown in Fig. 2e.

(1.87 Å) was shorter and with a higher density than that calculated for the DME oxygen atoms (ODME) in the DOL/DME electrolyte (1.97 Å), indicating that the Li+−HMPA solvation structure formed in the former electrolyte was more robust.
The relatively smaller solvation radius measured in the HMPA-containing electrolyte should result in faster Li+ transport kinetics, and thus a higher σ value.

The percentage of HMPA molecules that participated in the solvation structure in the DOL/HMPA- 6 electrolyte was higher than the analogous percentage of DME mole­ cules in the DOL/DME electrolyte (Fig.

Therefore, given a smaller fraction of HMPA in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte than that of DME in the DOL/DME electrolyte, there are less free HMPA molecules than free DME molecules in their corresponding electrolytes.
The changes in Li+ coordination number (n) as a function of Li−O distance for different electrolytes are shown in Fig. 2f.

Two results can be obtained from the data: (1) at distances of > 5 Å, the n attributed to HMPA in the DOL/ HMPA-6 electrolyte (black curve) increased less than the n attributed to DME in the DOL/DME electrolyte (blue); (2) the n attributed to TFSI− in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte (red) was higher than the value deter­ mined for the DOL/DME electrolyte (green).
These findings supported the hypothesis that the number of free HMPA molecules is lower and the quantity of CIPs and AGGs is higher in the HMPA-based electrolyte than in the control.
The Li+ solvation structures were further investigated using Raman spectroscopy.
A signal was observed at 624.1 cm−1 upon analysis of a mixture of HMPA (6 vol%) and DOL (Fig. 2g) and attributed to the bending vibration of the N−P−N bond in HMPA [45].
After LiTFSI (1 M) was dissolved in the mixture, the signal shifted to 644.3 cm−1 due to coordination of the Li+ with HMPA.
Raman signals that were assigned to TFSI−upon analysis of the DOL/HMPA-6 and DOL/DME electrolytes are shown in Fig. 2h and i.
The signals were deconvoluted to assess the quantities of AGGs, CIPs, and SSIPs present in the electrolytes.
The content of AGGs and CIPs in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte (83.7% in total) was found to be higher than that in the DOL/DME electrolyte (78.5%).
This result was supported by the radial relative density data (Fig. 2e) and can be attributed to a lower quantity of free HMPA molecules in the former.
Collectively, the theoretical and experimental data indicated that DOL/HMPA-6 featured a relatively low fraction of free HMPA and facilitated the formation of AGGs and CIPs.
As previ­ ously noted, these features were expected to not only suppress the pol­ ysulfide shuttle effect but also enhance the interfacial properties of Li anodes. 2.3.

Compatibility of the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte with Li metal electrodes The compatibility of the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte with Li metal electrodes was assessed using Li//Li symmetric cells that contained the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte.
As a control, Li//Li symmetric cells were also prepared with the DOL/DME electrolyte.
Rate capability data were measured at a plating/stripping capacity of 1 mAh cm−2 and current densities of 0.5, 1, 2, and 5 mA cm−2 for the different cells (Fig. 3a).
At each current density, the cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte displayed a smaller polarization voltage than the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte.
Similarly, the cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited a larger exchange current density than the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (0.22 vs. 0.12 mA cm−2) (Fig.
These results can be attributed to an enhanced σ and a higher tLi + pro­ vided by the former electrolyte.
The cycling stabilities of the different cells were measured at 1 mAh cm−2 and 1 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3b).

During the initial stage, the cell containing the DOL/HMPA electrolyte exhibited a polarization voltage of ca. 0.14 V, followed by reduction to ca. 0.05 V and then remained stable in the subsequent cycling test up to 600 h.
In contrast, the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte exhibited a noticeable fluctuation in the polarization voltage during the cycling test, with the observation of a maximum value of 0.11 V.

At an elevated current density of 5 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3c), the cell containing the DOL/ HMPA-6 electrolyte retained a relatively small polarization voltage (~0.06 V), which was only ca. one fourth of the values observed for the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (a maximum value of ~0.25 V was observed).

Compared to literature data, the cells reported herein are competitive in terms of rate capability and cycling stability (Table S1).
The chemical compositions of the SEI layers formed in the different electrolytes were investigated using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).

Inspection of the C 1s spectra (Fig. 3d and 3 g) revealed that C−C, C−O, C−F and CO3 2¡ species were present as their corresponding signals were observed at 284.8, 286.0, 292.6, and 289.2 eV, respectively [46].
The C−C and C−O species were attributed to decomposition of the ether-based solvents [47].
Likewise, the C−F species may stem from the partial decomposition of TFSI−[46].
The CO3 2¡ species corresponded to formation of lithium carbonate [25].
These data indicated that the SEI layer was composed of both organic and inorganic components.
The C−F species accounted for a lower fraction of the total C content present in the SEI layer formed in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte than that in the DOL/DME electrolyte (1.7% vs. 2.8%).
A similar result was gleaned from the F 1s XPS data (c.f., Fig. 3e and 3 h).
The C−F species accounted for a lower fraction of the total F content present in the SEI layer formed in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte as opposed to that in the DOL/DME electrolyte (82.0% vs. 94.3%).
The F 1s XPS data also indicated that a higher quantity of LiF was present in the SEI layer formed in the DOL/ HMPA-6 electrolyte as opposed to that in the DOL/DME electrolyte (18.0% vs. 5.7%).
A similar conclusion was drawn from the Li 1s XPS data (45.2% vs. 24.8%; c.f., Fig. 3f and 3i).
In other words, LiF, which enables SEI layers with high mechanical strength and high Li+ con­ ductivity [16], was more readily formed in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte than in the DOL/DME electrolyte.

The morphologies of the Li metal electrodes in the different elec­ trolytes were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
In the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte, the Li metal electrode adopted a smooth and compact surface (Fig. 3j).
This could be attributed to the LiF-rich SEI layer, which facilitated rapid Li+ transport and thus uniform Li depo­ sition on the surface of the metal electrode.
The compact and uniform LiF-rich SEI layer also prevented the side reactions between the Li electrode and the electrolyte as well as electrolyte consumption.
In contrast, a loose and noodle-like surface was observed upon inspection of the Li metal electrode that was exposed to the DOL/DME electrolyte (Fig. 3k).

The interfacial properties between the Li metal electrodes and the different electrolytes were assessed using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).

Before electrochemical cycling, each EIS plot featured a semicircle (Fig. 3l), where the intercept with the x-axis in the high frequency region and diameter of the semi­ circle corresponded to the serial resistance (Rs) of the cell and the charge transfer resistance (Rct) at the interface between the Li metal electrode and the electrolyte, respectively.
These values were obtained by fitting the EIS plots using the equivalent circuit shown in Fig.

The Li//Li symmetric cells containing the DOL/HMPA-6 or DOL/DME electrolyte were found to have similar Rs values (3.9 vs. 4.0 Ω), whereas the cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited a lower Rct value than the control (93.6 vs. 138.0 Ω).
The lower Rct value reflected more favorable charge transfer at the interface between the Li metal electrode and the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte.

The difference was ascribed to the formation of SEI layers on the surface of Li metal elec­ trodes.

The diameters of the semicircles in each plot pertain to the interface formed between the electrolyte and the SEI layer (denoted as RE-SEI) and the interface formed between the SEI layer and the Li metal electrode (denoted as RSEI-Li) [18].
The cell that contained the DOL/ HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited lower RE-SEI (11.0 vs. 17.4 Ω) and lower RSEI-Li (16.1 vs. 23.9 Ω) values than the control.

These results indicated that the formation of a LiF-rich SEI layer in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte enabled rapid Li+ transfer at the interface between the electrolyte and the Li electrodes, homogeneous Li plating/stripping, and fast electrode kinetics. 2.4.

Impact of the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte on sulfur cathodes To study how the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte affects sulfur cathodes over a charge/discharge cycle, the surface morphology of the sulfur cathode was investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
Coin-type Li–S cells that contained either the DOL/HMPA-6 or the DOL/ DME electrolyte were used.

After electrochemical cycling, the sulfur cathode in the cell that contained the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte was found to exhibit a porous surface (Fig. 4a) which matched that of its original (pre-cycled) morphology (Fig.

The morphological feature was ascribed to the presence of HMPA, which, due to its high DN, was expected to facilitate Li2S dissolution [50–52] and maintain the initial porous morphology of the sulfur cathode by facilitating a uniform deposition of Li2S [33].
In contrast, after electrochemical cycling, the surface of the sulfur cathode exposed to the DOL/DME electrolyte was found to be smooth and compact along with cracks (Fig. 4b).
Such morphology was attributed to two-dimensional Li2S deposition, which prevented further accessibility to the conductive host and the conduc­ tive reagents.

Collectively, the SEM data showed that the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte is effective at alleviating surface passivation and enhancing structural integrity of the sulfur cathode during charge/discharge cycling.
The interfacial properties of the electrodes in the Li–S cells were also evaluated using EIS.

As shown in Fig. 4c, a Li–S cell that contained the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited a lower Rct value than the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (29.0 vs. 55.5 Ω) before electro­ chemical cycling.
The smaller Rct value indicated that charge transfer at the electrode/electrolyte interface was more favorable in the DOL/ HMPA-6 electrolyte than in the DOL/DME electrolyte.
After electro­ chemical cycling (10 charge/discharge cycles at 0.1 C), each EIS plot was found to exhibit two semicircles (Fig. 4d).
Appearance of the second semicircle could be attributed to the formation of SEI layer on the Li anode.

The electrochemical impedances associated with the two semi­ circles were attributed to (1) the interface between the electrolyte and the electrode surface and (2) the interface between the newly formed SEI layer and the Li anode [53].
The key parameters of the EIS plots were obtained by fitting the data using an equivalent circuit (Fig.
The cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited lower impedance values (15.2 and 16.5 Ω) when compared with the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (34.7 and 22.2 Ω).
The lower impedance observed for the former could be ascribed to the porous morphology of the sulfur cathode and the LiF-rich SEI layer formed on the Li metal anode.
Visible cells were used to assess the polysulfide shuttle effect that occurred in the different electrolytes.

While the discharge profiles were recorded for the cells containing either the DOL/HMPA-6 or DOL/DME electrolyte (Fig. 5a), photos were taken at different discharge states (indicated in the discharge profiles) (Fig. 5b).

The cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited a specific capacity of 966.6 mAh g−1, a value that was more than two times higher than that measured for the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (420.0 mAh g−1).

Only a slight change in color was observed in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte, whereas a significant change from colorless to yellow green (indicative of the presence of polysulfides [54]) was observed in the DOL/DME electrolyte.
Moreover, the color change in the former occurred only during the initial period of discharge.
Thus, the polysulfide shuttle effect appeared to be significantly suppressed in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte, which manifested in the marked enhancement in device performance.

To quantitatively evaluate the polysulfide shuttle effect in the different electrolytes, the leakage current was measured for each cell (Fig.

The leakage current reflects the equilibrium between diffu­ sion of the polysulfides from the cathode to the anode due to a con­ centration gradient and migration of the polysulfides back to the cathode as driven by the applied electric field.

At 2.35 V, where the polysulfide shuttle effect occurred most severely, the leakage current value measured for the cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte was less than half of the value measured for the control (i.e., 0.57 vs. 1.4 mA g−1, respectively), indicating that the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte is effective at suppressing the shuttle effect. 2.5.

Likewise, two signals were observed at ca. 2.31 and 2.38 V in the anodic scan, corresponding to the oxidation of Li2S to lithium polysulfides and then to S8, respectively.
The redox signals measured for the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte were stronger than those measured for the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte.

This finding implied that sulfur was better utilized in the cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte due to the porous morphology of sulfur cathode than the sulfur in the cell con­ taining the DOL/DME electrolyte.

To quantify the Li+ transport prop­ erties of the sulfur cathodes in the Li–S cells containing the different electrolytes, a series of CV curves were collected at scan rates that ranged from 0.1 to 0.5 mV s−1 (Fig.
S11) and analyzed using the Randles−Sevcik equation [55,56].

The Li-ion diffusion coefficients measured for the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte were significantly higher than those measured for the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (c.f., 2.66 × 10−8 vs. 9.60 × 10−9 cm2 s−1 cor­ responding to peak C and 8.36 × 10−8 vs. 3.78 × 10−8 cm2 s−1 corre­ sponding to peak D).
Collectively, these data supported that the DOL/ HMPA-6 electrolyte facilitates sulfur cathode reaction kinetics.
The galvanostatic charge/discharge profiles recorded at 0.1 C (1 C = 1675 mA g−1) for the Li–S cells containing either the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte or the DOL/DME electrolyte are shown in Fig. 6b.
The charge and discharge plateaus were consistent with the oxidation and reduction signals observed in the CV profiles.
The Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte displayed a much higher specific capacity than the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (1374.9 and 1043.9 mAh g−1, respectively).

The ratio between the capacities corresponding to 2.12 and 2.29 V for the cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte (2.21) was closer to the theoretical value of 3 than that measured for the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (2.06).
This result indicated that the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte facilitated the conversion of poly­ sulfides to Li2S, leading to higher specific capacity of the Li–S cell.
Enlarged charge/discharge profiles of the regions that correspond to Li2S nucleation and Li2S decomposition, respectively, are shown in Fig. 6c and 6d.

During the discharge process, the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited a smaller overpotential (21 mV) that was attributed to favorable Li2S nucleation when compared to the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (34 mV).

When charging, the overpotential corresponding to Li2S decomposition was smaller for the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte (60 mV) than the value measured for the Li–S cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (91 mV).
Such favorable processes may stem from the Li+ solvation structure formed in the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte which facilitated the conversion between the polysulfides and Li2S in the sulfur cathode.
The rate capabilities of the Li–S cells containing the different elec­ trolytes were measured by increasing the current rate from 0.1 to 2 C (Fig. 6e).
At each current rate, the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited a higher specific capacity than the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte.

At 2 C, the specific capacity measured for the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte was 3.34 times higher than the value measured for the cell containing the DOL/DME electro­ lyte (606.4 vs. 181.5 mAh g−1).
When the current rate was reset back to 0.1 C, the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte recovered most of its initial capacity (939.2 mAh g−1 vs. an initial value of 1110.4 mAh g−1).

The cycling stabilities of the Li–S cells containing either the DOL/ HMPA-6 electrolyte or the DOL/DME electrolyte were measured at a current rate of 0.2 C since the polysulfide shuttle effect is exacerbated at low current rates [33].

As shown in Fig. 6f, the Li–S cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte initially exhibited a higher specific capacity than the cell containing the DOL/DME electrolyte (1101.0 vs. 882.4 mAh g−1, respectively).

After 300 cycles, the specific capacity measured for the cell containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte retained signifi­ cantly more of its initial value than the control (619.6 vs. 295.6 mAh g−1, respectively).
Similarly, the Li–S cells containing the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte also outperformed the cells that were prepared with other electrolytes reported in the literature (Table S2).
The significant enhancement in cycling stability can be attributed to the ability of HMPA to suppress the polysulfide shuttle effect. 3.

Conclusions We report that using a phosphoramide (i.e., HMPA) as co-solvent in electrolytes can overcome the longstanding issues associated with Li–S batteries, particularly the polysulfide shuttle effect and unwanted Li dendrite growth.

Theoretical and experimental data revealed that HMPA preferentially locates in the inner sheath of a Li+ solvation structure, which led to a reduced quantity of free HMPA molecules and effectively suppressed the polysulfide shuttle effect.
The use of HMPA also led to the formation of CIPs and AGGs that enabled the formation of LiF-rich SEI layers, which prevented the growth of Li dendrites.

As a result, the Li//Li symmetric cells that contained the DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte exhibited stable cycling for more than 600 h at 5 mA cm−2 and did so with a reduced polarization voltage that was only ca. 25% of the value recorded for a cell containing the conventional DOL/DME electrolyte.

The DOL/HMPA-6 electrolyte also afforded Li–S cells that delivered significantly enhanced specific capacity (606.4 vs. 181.5 mAh g−1 at 2 C) and cycling stability (619.6 vs. 295.2 mAh g−1 after 300 cycles at 0.2 C) when compared with analogous cells that were prepared with the conventional electrolyte.

The findings provide a means to bring Li–S batteries closer toward widespread practical use and the funda­ mental theory proposed may be adapted to bestow similar beneficial effects in other types of metal batteries. 4.

Preparation of the S@RGO cathode: Graphene oxide (GO) was synthesized using the modified Hummers’ method [1].
GO was converted into its reduced form (RGO) by chemical reduction using hydrazine hydrate, followed by thermal treatment.
First, a Teflon-lined autoclave (50 mL) was charged with a suspension of GO (20 mL, 5.62 mg mL1) and hydrazine hydrate (2.5 mL), and then placed an oven set at 180 °C for 12 h.
The product was collected by filtration, washed with deionized water, freeze-dried for 48 h, and then thermally treated using a tube furnace at 800 °C for 2 h under an atmosphere of Ar.
Sulfur was incorporated into the RGO by thermally annealing a mixture of sulfur and RGO (3:1, w/w) at 155 °C for 12 h [2].
The obtained composite was designated as S@RGO.

To prepare the S@RGO cathode, the S@RGO composite (40.24 mg), acetylene black (5.26 mg), and PVDF (5.06 mg) were ground using a mortar and pestle for 10 minutes, followed by dispersing the mixture in NMP (300 L) to form a S@RGO slurry.
The S@RGO cathode was prepared by coating the S@RGO slurry on Al foil and then dried in a vacuum oven set at 45 °C for 24 h.
Preparation of the electrolytes: The DOL/DME electrolyte was prepared by dissolving LiTFSI (2.8709 g, 10 mmol) and LiNO3 (0.2622 g, 2 wt%) in a mixture of DOL (5 mL) and DME (5 mL).
The DOL/HMPA electrolyte was prepared by dissolving LiTFSI (2.8709 g, 10 mmol) and LiNO3 (0.2622 g, 2 wt%) in a mixture of DOL and HMPA (10 mL in total).
The HMPA loading was 4 vol%, 6 vol%, 8 vol%, or 10 vol% and the resultant electrolytes were designated as DOL/HMPA-4, DOL/HMPA-6, DOL/HMPA-8, and DOL/HMPA-10, respectively.
All electrolytes were prepared in an Ar-filled glove box.
Characterization: SEM measurements were performed on a scanning electron microscope (Phenom, XL G2 Desktop) that operated at an accelerating voltage of 10 kV.
XPS data were collected on an X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, NEXSA) using monochromated Al K radiation (1486.7 eV).
The Raman spectra were obtained on a Raman microscope (Horiba Scientific, XploRA PLUS).

To prepare the samples that were characterized using SEM or XPS, the Li anode and the sulfur cathode were isolated after disassembling a tested Li//Li symmetric cell (after 5 charge/discharge cycles) and a tested Li−S cell (after 10 charge/discharge cycles), respectively.
The Li anode and sulfur cathode were washed with DOL to remove any impurities, followed by drying for 5 h in a glove box.
The electrochemical measurements were performed on an electrochemical workstation (Princeton, PMCCH808A) and a battery testing system (LAND, CT2100A).
The DN value of HMPA was measured using 23Na NMR spectrometry [3].

NaTFSI was first dissolved in a series of solvents, including acetonitrile (DN=14 kcal mol1), DME (DN=20 kcal mol1), pyridine (DN=33 kcal mol1), dimethyl sulfoxide (DN=30 kcal mol1), triethylamine (DN=55 kcal mol1), and HMPA.
The concentration of NaTFSI was 5 mmol L1.
A solution of NaCl in D2O (1 M) was sealed in a capillary tube (0.3 mm diameter) and used as an external reference.
The 23Na NMR shifts of NaTFSI in the different solvents were measured.
The DN value of HMPA was obtained by measuring the chemical shift of 23Na NMR signal followed by linear correlation to the DN value of the solvent (see Figure S1).
Electrochemical measurements: The ion conductivity values of the different electrolytes were measured using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).

Stainless steel//stainless steel symmetric cells were prepared using stainless steel discs as the electrodes, a polyimide (PI) ring spacer (inner diameter = 10 mm, outer diameter = 16 mm, thickness = 0.125 mm) as the separator, and either the DOL/HMPA electrolyte or the DOL/DME electrolyte (20 μL).
EIS data were collected on an electrochemical workstation by applying a sine wave with an amplitude of 10 mV over a frequency ranged from 105 to 0.1 Hz.

The ion conductivity value (, S cm−1) was calculated using the following equation: where I and S represent the thickness and the area of the hole of the PI separator, respectively, and R represents the resistance ().
R can be obtained from the intercept of the Nyquist plot with the x-axis.

The activation energy (Ea) required for Li+ transport in the DOL/HMPA-6 or DOL/DME electrolyte was estimated using the Arrhenius equation: where , T, A, and R represent ion conductivity, the absolute temperature, a pre-exponential constant. and the standard gas constant (8.314 J mol−1 K−1), respectively [4,5].
Li//Li symmetric cells were prepared using Li foils as the electrodes, PP membranes as separator, and either the DOL/HMPA or the DOL/DME electrolyte (40 μL).
The rate capability and cycling stability tests of the Li//Li symmetric cells were performed on a battery testing system.
The rate capability was tested at a current density that ranged from 0.5 to 5 mA cm−1 with a plating/stripping capacity of 1 mAh cm−2.
The cycling stability was measured at a current density of 1 or 5 mA cm−2 with a plating/stripping capacity of 1 mAh cm−2.

Tafel plots for the Li//Li symmetric cells were obtained from the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) data, which were collected at a scan rate that ranged from 0.1 mV s−1 from 0.2 V to −0.2 V on an electrochemical workstation.
The exchange current density (i0) values were calculated using the Tafel equation: where η and i represent the potential and current, respectively.
The i0 value is obtained as the current density at the intersection of the anodic and the cathodic polarization curves.
The Li+ transference number was measured via the chronoamperometry method using Li//Li symmetric cells [3].
The chronoamperometry tests were performed on an electrochemical workstation.
The I−t curves were obtained by applying a constant voltage of 10 mV.

The Li+ transference number (tLi+) was calculated using the following equation: where V represents the voltage applied, I0 and Is represent the initial current and the stabilized current, respectively, and R0 and Rs represent the charge transfer resistance of the Li//Li symmetric cell before and after the chronoamperometry test, respectively.
The R0 and Rs values were obtained from the EIS measurement.
Li−S cells were prepared using the S@RGO cathode, a PP membrane as the separator, Li foil as the anode, and either the DOL/HMPA-6 or the DOL/DME electrolyte (40 μL).
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves and EIS data of Li−S cells were obtained on an electrochemical workstation.
Charge/discharge, rate capability and cycling stability data of Li−S cells were obtained on a battery testing system.

To measure the leakage current, a Li−S cell was subjected to an initial discharge/charge cycle over a potential range of 1.7 and 2.7 V, followed by discharging to 1.7 V and then being charging at a constant potential of 2.2, 2.35, 2.4, 2.5, or 2.6 V for 20 h.
The stabilized current was considered as the leakage current.

The Li-ion diffusion coefficients () of the Li−S cells that contained DOL/HMPA-6 or DOL/DME electrolyte were obtained from the plots of Ip versus the square root of v following the Randles−Sevcik equation [2,6]: where Ip, n, A, , and v represent the redox signal peak current, the number of electrons involved in the electrochemical reaction (n = 2 for Li−S batteries), the electrode area, the Li-ion concentration in the electrolyte, and the scan rate used, respectively.
The visible cells were assembled using the S@RGO cathode, a PP membrane as the separator, Li foil as the anode, and either the DOL/HMPA-6 or DOL/DME electrolyte (10 mL).
The assembly and measurement of the visible cells were performed in an Ar-filled glovebox.
Molecular Dynamics: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed in this study.

The Gaussian code was employed to calculate the coordination structures and binding strengths of Li+ with different solvent molecules, electrostatic potential, and the energy levels of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO).

The binding strengths were calculated using the following the equation: E = Etotal−Eion−Esol, where Etotal, Eion, and Esol are the total energy of solvent coordinated with Li+, the energy of Li+, and the energy of solvent, respectively.
The DFT calculations were carried out at the B3LYP level with the 6-311G(d,p) basis set.

MD simulations were performed using a large-scale atomic/molecular massively parallel simulator code, and the interatom interaction was described by the all-atom optimized potentials for liquid simulations force field.
The velocity-verlet algorithm with a fixed time step of 0.5 fs was used to integrate the equations of motion.
To estimate the Li+ solvation structures in the two kinds of electrolytes, Li+ and solvent molecules, in ratios similar to those used in the experiments, were randomly placed in the simulation box.
The electrolytes were then minimized with the steepest descent method, followed by 50-ns simulation under the isothermal–isobaric ensemble (NPT) at the temperature of 298 K and pressure of 1 atm.
The O radial relative density was calculated based on the relaxed structure.

The saturated coordination structures of Li+ formed with different solvents were calculated from the O radial relative density using the following formula: where CN(r) represents the saturated coordination number, ρ represents the number density of the solvent molecules, g(r) represents the O radial relative density, and r represents the distance from Li+.
